did_you_know.text: Did you know? Hezekiah removed the high places, smashed the sacred pillars, and cut down the Asherah pole. He also broke into pieces the bronze snake Moses had made, because the Israelites had been burning incense to it; he called it Nehushtan.
Did you know? The text emphasizes that Hezekiah trusted in the Lord more than any of the kings of Judah who came before him, describing him as a king unlike any who had come before or after him.
Did you know? Because he remained devoted to the Lord, Hezekiah prospered in everything he undertook. He also rebelled against the king of Assyria and refused to serve him.
Did you know? Hezekiah extended his rule as far as the region of Gaza and defeated the Philistines as far as their borders.

Did you know? During Hezekiah’s reign, Shalmaneser king of Assyria came against Samaria and besieged it. According to the account in this chapter, the siege began in the fourth year of Hezekiah’s reign.
Did you know? After conquering Samaria, the king of Assyria deported the Israelites to Assyria and settled them in Halah, by the Habor River, in Gozan, and in the cities of the Medes.
Did you know? In the fourteenth year of Hezekiah’s reign, Sennacherib king of Assyria attacked all the fortified cities of Judah and captured them.

Did you know? After Hezekiah paid the tribute, the king of Assyria sent the Tartan, the Rabsaris, and the Rabshakeh with a large army to Jerusalem. They came to the conduit of the Upper Pool, near the road to the Washerman’s Field.
Did you know? Hezekiah’s officials asked the Rabshakeh to speak to them in Aramaic rather than in Hebrew, so that the people on the wall would not hear what he was saying.

Did you know? The Rabshakeh tried to undermine the confidence of the people of Jerusalem. He urged them to surrender, promised them a good land, and mocked their belief that the Lord would save the city. The people remained silent, and Hezekiah’s officials returned to him with their clothes torn.
